title: Book 7 — Polymnia, Chapter 10
paragraphs: When Mardonius had thus smoothed over the resolution Xerxes had expressed, he fell silent. The other Persians said nothing, not venturing to declare an opinion contrary to the one proposed. Then Artabanus son of Hystaspes, who was Xerxes's uncle and relied on that relationship, spoke as follows: “O king, if opinions opposed to one another are not spoken, it is impossible to pick the better by comparison — one simply has to accept what has been said; but if opposite opinions are uttered, such a choice becomes possible. Just as we cannot tell pure gold by itself, but when we rub it on the touchstone beside other gold we distinguish the better, so it is with counsel. Now I advised your father Darius, who was my brother, not to march against the Scythians, a people who held no settled city anywhere on earth. He, expecting to subdue these nomad Scythians, would not listen to me; he marched, and came back from the campaign having lost many brave men from his army. You, O king, are planning to march against men who are far better than the Scythians — men reported to be excellent both on sea and on land. What is to be feared in this undertaking it is right that I should declare to you. You say you will yoke the Hellespont with a bridge and march an army through Europe to Greece. Now suppose we are defeated either on land or on sea — or on both — for the men are reported to be brave in combat, and we may judge for ourselves that it is so, seeing that the Athenians by themselves destroyed that great army which came with Datis and Artaphernes to Attica. Suppose, however, that they do not win on both elements; even so, if they attack our fleet and defeat us in a sea-battle, then sail to the Hellespont and break the bridge — this alone, O king, will prove a great peril. It is not by any special wisdom of my own that I suspect this might happen; I am only imagining the sort of disaster that nearly befell us the last time, when your father, having yoked the Thracian Bosphorus and bridged the Ister, had crossed to attack the Scythians. On that occasion the Scythians used every kind of entreaty to persuade the Ionians, to whom the guarding of the Ister bridges had been entrusted, to break the passage. At that time, if Histiaeus the tyrant of Miletus had gone along with the opinion of the other tyrants, and had not opposed them, the whole Persian power would have been destroyed. Yet it is frightful even to say that the king's entire empire came to depend on one human being. Do not, then, of your own free will walk into such a danger when there is no need. Do as I say: dissolve this assembly for now; and later, at whatever time seems good to you, when you have considered the matter prudently with yourself, declare what you think best. I hold good counsel to be a very great gain; for even if something goes wrong, the counsel that was taken is no worse for having been defeated by fortune, while the man who took bad counsel at first, even if fortune goes along with him, has simply stumbled onto a lucky prize — his counsel was bad all the same. You see how God strikes with thunderbolts those creatures which stand above the rest, and does not allow them to make a proud show; while the small ones provoke no jealousy in him. You see also how he hurls his bolts always at the tallest buildings and the tallest trees; for God is in the habit of cutting short whatever stands above the rest. So too a large army may be destroyed by a small one in some such way as this: when God, having grown envious, casts on them panic or thunder from heaven, they are utterly destroyed, unworthily of their merit; for God does not suffer anyone but himself to have proud thoughts. Haste in any matter breeds disasters, out of which great losses are apt to come; but in waiting there are many good things contained, which, even if they do not appear good at first, will be found so in time. That, O king, is my counsel to you. And you, son of Gobryas, Mardonius — stop speaking foolish words about the Greeks, since they in no way deserve to be spoken of slightingly. By slandering the Greeks you are stirring up the king himself to make this expedition, and I think that is the very end to which you are bending all your efforts. Let it not be so. Slander is a most grievous thing: in it the wrongdoers are two, and the injured party is one. The slanderer does wrong because he speaks against someone not present; the other because he is persuaded of the thing before he has certain knowledge of it; and the man who is not there when the words are spoken suffers wrong both ways — he has been slandered by the one and judged wicked by the other. However, if we really must campaign against these men, then let the king himself stay behind in the Persian homeland, and let the two of us lay our own sons as stakes for the wager. You yourself lead out the army, choosing the men you want and taking as large a force as you please. If things turn out for the king as you promise, let my sons be put to death, and let me be put to death along with them; but if it goes as I predict, let your sons suffer this, and you yourself along with them, if indeed you return. If you are not willing to submit to this test, but will at any cost lead an army against Greece, then I say that those of us left behind in this country will hear that Mardonius, after bringing great calamity on the Persians, is being torn by dogs and birds of prey — either in the land of the Athenians, or perhaps in the land of the Lacedaemonians (unless indeed this has already happened to you on the way) — and that you have finally learned what kind of men these are, whom you are urging the king to march against.”
